text: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, born on 15 April 1930 in Reykjavík, is an Icelandic politician who served as the fourth president of Iceland from 1980 to 1996, making her the first woman to hold the position and the first in the world to be democratically elected president of a country. She served for 16 years, becoming the longest-serving elected female head of state in history. Her father, Finnbogi Rútur Þorvaldsson, was a civil engineer, and her mother, Sigríður Eiríksdóttir, was a nurse who led the national nurses association. The following year, her younger brother Þorvaldur was born but died in childhood after drowning in Hreðavatn. She studied English and French literature with a focus on plays at the University of Grenoble and later the Sorbonne, graduating in 1953. In 1954, she married and began acting, co-founding a theatre group and translating French plays. She studied theatre history at the University of Copenhagen from 1957 to 1958, was divorced in 1963, and participated in anti-military rallies during the 1960s and 1970s opposing the United States military presence in Iceland. In 1972, she adopted a daughter, becoming the first single woman in Iceland to do so. That same year, she began teaching French on television for RÚV and was appointed artistic director of the Reykjavík Theatre Company. She joined the Advisory Committee on Cultural Affairs in the Nordic Countries in 1976 and became its chair in 1978, holding these roles until her presidency began in 1980. She also worked as a French teacher at various colleges, including the University of Iceland, and as a tour guide with the Icelandic Tourist Bureau, eventually becoming its head. In the 1980 presidential election, she ran to demonstrate women's capability in political leadership and did not expect to win; she won with 33.6% of the vote on 29 June 1980, taking office on 1 August 1980. The vote was split among four candidates. Her election marked the first time a woman was democratically elected as a head of state globally, and it led to a significant increase in the number of women in the Althing. She was re-elected without opposition in 1984 and 1992. In 1986, she oversaw the Reykjavík Summit between U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, which improved Cold War relations. In 1988, she became the first incumbent president to face a challenger, winning with 92.7% of the vote. Though the Icelandic presidency is largely ceremonial, Vigdís used it actively to shape national identity through cultural initiatives. She is an environmentalist who advocated for reforestation and prevention of topsoil loss, a pacifist who describes herself as a "peace person," and an advocate for gay rights. In 1994, during the debate on joining the European Economic Area, she faced strong opposition but supported European integration and refused to use her presidential veto, a decision she considered the most difficult of her career. She decided not to run for a fifth term and stepped down in August 1996 after 16 years, remaining the longest-serving female elected head of state in recorded history. In 1996, she became the founding chair of the Council of Women World Leaders; from 1997 to 2001, she served as the first chair of the World Commission on the Ethics in Scientific Knowledge and Technology. Since 1998, she has been UNESCO's Goodwill Ambassador for languages and is a member of the Fondation Chirac's honour committee. After leaving office, she continued her peace advocacy, expressing in 2016 a desire for the United States and Russia to visit Iceland to resolve their differences through dialogue, describing their relations as a new Cold War. She is also a member of the Club of Madrid.
